prompt: Which method tells you how many elements an `ArrayList` holds?
hint: An array has a field for this; a list has a method.

choices.text: `length`
choices.why: That is an array's field; a list has no `length`.

choices.text: `size()`
choices.why: Right: it printed 3 for the three titles.

choices.text: `capacity()`
choices.why: The capacity is the length of the array inside, and `ArrayList` does not expose it.

choices.text: `count()`
choices.why: There is no such method on `List`.

prompt: A list holds `[Dom Casmurro, Iracema]`. What does `titles.add(0, "O Cortiço")` leave?
hint: The index is where the new element goes.

choices.text: `[O Cortiço, Iracema]`, replacing the first
choices.why: Replacing is `set`; `add` inserts and moves the others along.

choices.text: `[O Cortiço, Dom Casmurro, Iracema]`
choices.why: Right: inserted at index 0, the others moved one place.

choices.text: `[Dom Casmurro, Iracema, O Cortiço]`, because `add` always appends
choices.why: Only `add(x)` appends; `add(i, x)` inserts at `i`.

prompt: `List<Integer> pages` holds `[10, 20, 30, 1]`. What does `pages.remove(1)` remove?
hint: Two methods are called `remove`, and the literal `1` is an `int`.

choices.text: The number 1, at the end
choices.why: That needs `remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`; the plain `1` chose the other method.

choices.text: The 20, at index 1
choices.why: Right: `remove(int index)` matches an `int` without boxing, so it wins.

choices.text: Both the 20 and the 1
choices.why: Each call removes one element.

choices.text: Nothing; the compiler refuses an ambiguous call
choices.why: It is not ambiguous to the compiler; the exact `int` match is chosen.

prompt: `titles.get(5)` on a list of two titles. What happens?
hint: A list checks its index as an array does.

choices.text: `IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 2`
choices.why: Right: the program ended on it, naming both numbers.

choices.text: It returns `null`
choices.why: A list never answers a bad index with `null`.

choices.text: The list grows to six elements and returns `null`
choices.why: Lists grow on `add`, never on `get`.

prompt: `List<int>` does not compile; a list of whole numbers is written `List<___>`.
hint: The wrapper class from lesson 4.

prompt: `titles.remove("Iracema")` found the element to remove. How?
hint: Lesson 24 is about the method it calls.

choices.text: By comparing references with `==`
choices.why: Two equal strings may be two objects; the list compares with `equals`.

choices.text: By its position, remembered from when it was added
choices.why: A list keeps no record of what was added where, beyond the order itself.

choices.text: By calling `equals` on each element in turn
choices.why: Right: which is why `equals` has to be overridden correctly for your own classes.

prompt: What is inside an `ArrayList`?
hint: Section 03's first sentence after the heading.

choices.text: A chain of nodes, each pointing at the next
choices.why: That is a linked list, which lesson 32 compares.

choices.text: An array, and a count of the slots in use
choices.why: Right: the size is the count, the capacity the array's length.

choices.text: A hash table keyed by index
choices.why: Index lookup goes straight to an array slot; no hashing is involved.

prompt: The capacity went 10, 15, 22, 33, 49, 73. What is the next capacity after 73?
hint: The old length plus half of it, rounded down.

prompt: Why does `java Growth` fail without `--add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED`?
hint: The message names a module.

choices.text: Because `elementData` does not exist in Java 25
choices.why: It exists; the message names it and refuses to open it.

choices.text: `java.base` does not open `java.util` to code outside it
choices.why: Right: lesson 40 explains it; the flag opens the package for this one run.

choices.text: Because reflection is disabled unless the program runs as root
choices.why: Nothing about users is involved; the refusal is the module's.

choices.text: Because `setAccessible` only works on fields of your own classes
choices.why: It works on your own and on opened packages, which is what the flag adds.

prompt: A program knows a list will hold a million elements. What does `new ArrayList<>(1_000_000)` save?
hint: What happens at each step of the growth?

choices.text: Nothing: the capacity grows to a million either way
choices.why: It ends in the same place, but the steps on the way each copied the whole array.

choices.text: Memory, because the list then stores `int` instead of `Integer`
choices.why: The elements are `Integer` objects whatever the capacity.

choices.text: Every replacement of the array, and the copying that comes with each
choices.why: Right: the array is the right size from the start, so no step happens.

choices.text: The time of each `get`, which no longer checks the index
choices.why: `get` checks the index whatever the capacity.

prompt: Adding 100,000 numbers took 26 ms at the end and 492 ms at the front. Why is the front slower?
hint: What has to happen before index 0 is free?

choices.text: Every insert first moves all the others along
choices.why: Right: the work grows with the list, where an append writes one slot.

choices.text: The array is replaced on every insert at the front
choices.why: It is replaced only when full, whichever end you add at.

choices.text: Index 0 is checked twice
choices.why: The check costs the same at any index.

prompt: Which of these were true of the capacities `Growth` printed? Choose all that apply.
hint: Seven lines: from size 1 to size 74.

choices.text: The first `add` gave the list a capacity of 10
choices.why: Yes: `size 1: capacity 10`.

choices.text: Each capacity was about one and a half times the one before
choices.why: Yes: old plus half of old.

choices.text: The capacity doubled each time
choices.why: 15 is not 20; the factor is one and a half.

choices.text: The capacity grew by one with every add
choices.why: That is the size; the capacity stayed put between steps.

prompt: A sensor writes a million `double` readings, and the count never changes. Which does section 04 choose?
hint: Fixed size, primitive elements.

choices.text: `List<Double>`, because lists are the default
choices.why: The default has an exception for exactly this case: a million boxed doubles cost a million objects.

choices.text: `double[]`
choices.why: Right: fixed size and primitives, stored side by side.

choices.text: `Arrays.asList` over a `double[]`
choices.why: That wraps the array as a list of one element, the array itself; it is not a list of doubles.

prompt: `List<String> view = Arrays.asList(shelf);` then `view.set(0, "O Cortiço")`. What happened to `shelf`?
hint: Does `asList` copy?

choices.text: Nothing, because `asList` copied the array into a new list
choices.why: It did not copy: the array printed the new title.

choices.text: It was refused with `UnsupportedOperationException`
choices.why: `set` worked; only changing the size was refused.

choices.text: Its first element became *O Cortiço*
choices.why: Right: the list is a view of the array, so writes go through to it.

prompt: Which list accepts `add`?
hint: Two of these cannot change size.

choices.text: `List.of("a", "b")`
choices.why: It refuses every change.

choices.text: `Arrays.asList("a", "b")`
choices.why: It cannot grow: the array behind it has a fixed length.

choices.text: `new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"))`
choices.why: Right: an ordinary growing list, filled from the fixed one.

choices.text: `List.copyOf(List.of("a", "b"))`
choices.why: `copyOf` also returns an unmodifiable list.

prompt: Match each way of making a list to what it allows.
hint: Section 04's last program.

pairs.right: set only, writing through to the array

prompt: Why does the section call it a weakness that `List.of` and `ArrayList` share one interface?
hint: What does the type tell a caller?

choices.text: Because the two print differently
choices.why: Both print `[a, b]`; printing is not the issue.

choices.text: The type has `add`, and only running it says whether it works
choices.why: Right: a `List` parameter does not say which methods will be refused.

choices.text: Because `List.of` is slower to read than `ArrayList`
choices.why: Reading is not what differs; changing is.

prompt: An `ArrayList` holding 15 elements is full, and `add` is called. Put what happens in order.
hint: Make room, then write.
items: A new array of length 22 is created
The 15 elements are copied into it
The list's field points at the new array
The new element is written at index 15 and the size becomes 16

prompt: A method receives `List<String> titles` and calls `titles.add("x")`. Callers sometimes pass `List.of(...)`. What should the method do?
hint: Whose list is it?

choices.text: Catch `UnsupportedOperationException` and ignore it
choices.why: Then the title is silently not added, which is the worst outcome.

choices.text: Copy into its own `new ArrayList<>(titles)` and add to that
choices.why: Right: it no longer depends on what kind of list it was given, and the caller's list is untouched.

choices.text: Cast `titles` to `ArrayList` before adding
choices.why: `List.of` is not an `ArrayList`; the cast throws `ClassCastException`.

prompt: A queue of waiting members keeps taking the first member out with `remove(0)`. What does section 03 say about that?
hint: Removing at the front moves the rest.

choices.text: It is as fast as removing at the end, since the index is known
choices.why: It moves every remaining element one place back.

choices.text: Each removal shifts the rest; `ArrayDeque` fits better
choices.why: Right: the cost grows with the length of the queue.

choices.text: It shrinks the array by half on each removal to save memory
choices.why: An `ArrayList` does not shrink its array on removal.
